Parent
PAIR-ent
n. (a father or mother; rendering Greek goneus)
From Latin parens, from parere, to bring forth. The Greek goneus is built the same way, from ginomai — the parent is the one from whom the child came, and Scripture makes that fact the ground of an obligation.

Biblical Definition

A parent in Scripture holds an office, not merely a relationship, and the fifth commandment attaches to it the first promise: honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long. Paul restates it as the basic ordering of a Christian household: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1) — and the ground he gives is not utility but rightness, the creational fitness of the thing. The duty runs both ways and Paul states the parental side memorably: “the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children” (2 Corinthians 12:14), which he uses to explain why he took no money from the Corinthians. Provision flows downward, honour flows upward, and a household that reverses either is disordered. The Lord Jesus qualifies the obedience without abolishing it — the disciple who loves father or mother more than Him is not worthy of Him, and He warns that the gospel will divide households, with children delivered up by parents (Luke 21:16). And Paul makes disobedience to parents a diagnostic of civilisational decay, listing it among the marks of the last days: “men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:2) — sandwiched between blasphemy and ingratitude, which is where Scripture thinks it belongs.

Webster 1828 Definition

A father or mother, holding an office. Children are to obey because it is right; parents lay up for children rather than the reverse; and disobedience to parents is listed among the marks of the last days.

expand to see more

PARENT, n. [L. parens, from pario, to bear.] A father or mother; he or she that produces young.

2. That which produces; cause; source; as idleness is the parent of vice.

PARENTAL, a. Pertaining to parents; as parental authority.

3. Becoming parents; tender; affectionate; as parental care.

4. Disobedient to parents, a mark of the perilous times. 2 Tim. 3.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 6:1 — "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right."

2 Corinthians 12:14 — "Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children."

2 Timothy 3:2 — "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,"

Luke 21:16 — "And ye shall be betrayed both by parents, and brethren, and kinsfolks, and friends; and some of you shall they cause to be put to death."

Modern Corruption

Parental authority has been steadily transferred to the state and to the expert class, on the premise that children belong first to society; and inside the church the same commandment is sometimes pressed into a demand for adult obedience it never made.

expand to see more

Scripture assigns the raising of children to parents and to no one else: fathers are to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4), and the commands of Deuteronomy 6 place the teaching of God's word in the house, on the road, at bedtime and at rising. Family, church, and state are three God-ordained authorities with distinct spheres, and the modern drift — in which schooling, medical decisions, and the moral formation of children pass by default to institutions that hold a different account of the good — is a sphere violation whatever its intentions. The dictionary holds the classical position: the state bears a genuine and God-given sword, including against parents who abuse their charge, and it has no commission to replace the household as the child's formative authority.

The opposite abuse belongs to the church and appears wherever the fifth commandment is preached as unlimited. The commandment says honour, and honour is owed lifelong; Paul's word to children is obey, and it is addressed to children under the roof and qualified in the Lord. An adult son owes his father honour, care in age (which the Lord Jesus enforced against the corban evasion in Mark 7:11-13), and a hearing; he does not owe him obedience in the disposal of his own household, and no parent may command what God forbids. Where a movement teaches otherwise — adult children under paternal authority indefinitely, marriages arranged and vetoed — it has taken a real commandment past the point Scripture set for it, and the households it has damaged are the evidence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek goneus (a parent, from ginomai, to come into being); Hebrew uses ab (father) and em (mother) rather than a collective term, which is itself significant — the commandment names them separately.

expand to see more

Greek goneus (G1118) — a parent; the word in Ephesians 6:1, 2 Corinthians 12:14, 2 Timothy 3:2, and Luke 21:16.

Hebrew ab (H1) — father; the first term of the fifth commandment and the root of abba.

Hebrew em (H517) — mother; named alongside the father in the commandment, with equal claim to honour.

Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; the verb of the fifth commandment, whose root sense is to give weight to.

Greek hypakouo (G5219) — to listen under, obey; the verb in Ephesians 6:1, distinct from the honour owed lifelong.

Usage

"“Obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right” — the ground is creational fitness, and the qualifier is real."

"“The parents for the children” — provision runs downward; Paul uses it to explain refusing Corinthian money."

"“Disobedient to parents” — listed between blasphemy and ingratitude as a mark of the last days."
